transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-15
Time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 30 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Recruiter), Liam Chen (Engineering Manager), Alyssa Martin (Candidate)

Summary: Initial recruiting screen to cover background, experience with model serving/inference, interests, and logistics.

[00:00] Maya: Hi Alyssa, thanks for taking the time, can you hear us okay?

[00:05] Alyssa: Yeah, hi Maya, hi Liam, I can hear you. Thanks for setting this up.

[00:10] Maya: Awesome. I'm Maya, I'm the recruiter on this role. Liam here is the hiring manager. We'll do a quick intro, cover your background, some experience questions, and talk next steps. About 30 minutes. Sound good?

[00:22] Alyssa: Sounds great.

[00:28] Liam: Hey Alyssa, quick intro from me - I'm Liam, I lead the infra team that owns the inference runtime and deployment platform. Curious about your recent work at Onyx AI and specifically things you ran in production.

[00:40] Alyssa: Sure. At Onyx I was a senior infra engineer focused on model serving and orchestration. I worked on a custom serving layer for transformer models, helped ship quantized variants, and did a lot of work on batching and KV cache correctness. We moved from a pod-per-request approach to a pooled runtime which cut token cost by around 30 percent.

[01:05] Liam: Nice. When you say pooling, do you mean a shared process that keeps model weights resident and services multiple requests concurrently?

[01:12] Alyssa: Yeah, exactly. We had long-lived worker processes on GPUs with an LRU-ish shard assignment. We also implemented prefix caching for repeated conversation contexts and a small adaptive batching algorithm - nothing too fancy but tuned for our tail latency SLOs.

[01:28] Maya: Walk me through a typical day - are you hands-on with code, or more design/PR review?

[01:34] Alyssa: Mostly hands-on. I write Python and some C++ / CUDA hooks for performance-sensitive parts. I also own production incidents sometimes and run postmortems. On the hiring side I mentored juniors but wasn't running interviews full-time.

[01:45] Liam: Do you have exposure to private deployments or VPC setups? We run hybrid, so we care about on-prem/security requirements.

[01:52] Alyssa: Yes, we had an enterprise offering where customers wanted VPC peering and strict egress controls. I helped implement IAM roles for job submission and integrated our service with customers' KMS for model key wrapping. I don't recall the exact HSM vendor, but we did KMS integrations and audit logging.

[02:10] Maya: Any experience with SOC2 or compliance audits?

[02:14] Alyssa: I participated in SOC2 readiness reviews - mostly about logging, RBAC, and data retention policies. I worked with security to ensure logs were forwarded to a central SIEM and we had retention windows configurable per customer.

[02:27] Liam: Technical question: how do you reason about latency SLOs vs batching for throughput? Any heuristics you used?

[02:33] Alyssa: We had a tiered policy: for low-latency routes we'd cap batching window aggressively and accept lower GPU utilization; for high-throughput background jobs we increased the window and used qps-based autoscaling. We also ran A/B tests to measure quality regressions from quantized models, since sometimes FP16->INT8 hurt certain prompts.

[02:55] Liam: Did you run regression benchmarks with eval suites? How automated was that?

[02:58] Alyssa: Fairly automated. We had nightly evals and a promotion pipeline that would gate a model variant if specific metric deltas exceeded thresholds. The infra would also trigger canary rollouts for a few clients.

[03:12] Maya: Are you comfortable writing a short take-home? We usually have a light coding exercise or a short systems writeup.

[03:18] Alyssa: Yep, that's fine.

[03:20] Liam: For the coding part, any preferences? We can do Python-focused question around asynchronous request batching or a system-design prompt.

[03:29] Alyssa: I prefer something that mirrors the role - maybe implement a simple batched inference simulator with async APIs, or a small design doc on caching strategies.

[03:36] Maya: Great. A couple of quick clarifying things - what's your current notice period and comp expectations?

[03:43] Alyssa: I'm on a one-month notice. For comp, I'm targeting in the low to mid six figures, depending on equity and role level.

[03:51] Liam: That aligns with the band for senior infra eng.

[03:55] Maya: Any constraints on interview timing next week?

[03:58] Alyssa: I'm mostly open afternoons PST except Wednesday morning.

[04:04] Liam: Cool. A few deeper technical checks - where did you touch model compilation / kernel selection? Did you ever tune kernels or fallback strategies?

[04:12] Alyssa: I collaborated with our ML team; I didn't write CUDA kernels from scratch but I wired up kernel selection logic, heuristic rules for sequence length, and a simple registry of optimized ops. On one project we fell back to a reference kernel when a quantized path failed and that was fine for a small percentage of traffic.

[04:32] Liam: Any experience with cost telemetry per token or per route? We care a lot about unit economics.

[04:37] Alyssa: Yes, I helped build a cost dashboard that attributed GPU time per request and token counts, and we tied it back to the routing rules so we could reroute cheaper model variants for certain non-sensitive routes.

[04:51] Maya: Behavior / culture question - how do you handle ambiguous ownership across teams?

[04:56] Alyssa: I try to establish a clear RACI early; if it's cross-functional I push to get a short kickoff doc that defines the owner for each area. If disputes come up, I escalate to the manager with a proposal and options.

[05:12] Liam: Ok, final quick screen: do you have a coding sample or GitHub we can review?

[05:17] Alyssa: Yeah, I can share a repo with a toy batching service and some infra scripts - I'll send the link after this call.

[05:23] Maya: Perfect. Anything you want to ask about the role or team?

[05:27] Alyssa: What's the current team size and what will be the first major project?

[05:31] Liam: The infra team is 10 engineers; for this role you'd be on the serving runtime sub-team working on batching, caching, and model rollout. First big project will be improving caching policies and supporting a new quantized model family.

[05:46] Alyssa: Sounds exciting.

[05:49] Maya: Great. We'll send the take-home, and if that looks good we'll schedule a technical interview. Any constraints on timeframe?

[05:56] Alyssa: Two weeks would be ideal, but I can be flexible.

[06:00] Maya: Awesome. Thanks so much, Alyssa. We'll follow up with next steps.

[06:05] Alyssa: Thank you both.

[06:07] Maya: Quick outro - recap next steps: Maya will send the take-home and rubric; Liam will propose times for the technical loop; Alyssa will send GitHub link.

[06:18] Alyssa: Yep. Thanks.

[06:20] End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcript had a few misheard terms (HSM vendor, some kernel names), speaker turns occasionally merged.
